designs.title: How Beer Is Made
designs.why: The cleanest file of the three: solid, even line weight, it will print without trouble, and white on black reads well. But it's an infographic. Nine boxes, arrows and a default geometric sans make it look like a brewery-tour giveaway or a textbook page, not a $50 back print. From 3 m it's a grey grid with no focal point and no attitude, and the captions are only legible up close.
designs.fix: Make one hero illustration (the brew kettle or fermenter, drawn large) and turn the seven steps into a small numbered list or ring around it in a typeface with character. Cut the explanatory sentences.

designs.title: Gin Botanicals
designs.why: The best concept and the best layout: a staggered plate, a classic italic and good negative space. It reads as considered on a white tee. At full size, though, the engraving has broken up into autotrace noise: broken dotted contours, specks, crumbly shading on the juniper berries and orris. It looks like a bad thresholded scan, not an engraving, and those fine specks will either plug or drop out in screen print.
designs.fix: Redraw or clean the linework as true engraving: closed contours, hatching with deliberate line direction, no isolated specks below about 0.3 mm. Keep the composition and type exactly as they are.

designs.title: Vineyard
designs.why: The scene is nice and the small spaced serif is tasteful. But the whole rectangle is packed edge to edge with the same mottled dot-dash texture, so from 3 m it reads as a grey slab with no light, depth or focal point. Up close the lines are broken and noisy, like a threshold trace, not cut lines. It looks like a wine-label stock image and has no hook for the buyer.
designs.fix: Rebuild it with real tonal hierarchy: open the sky and the path to bare shirt, give the farmhouse and cypresses clean, bold contour work, and let the scene vignette out at the edges instead of filling a hard rectangle.
